name: Bertrand Russell
role: British philosopher, logician and political activist (1872-1970)
summary: Russell was a liberal-socialist internationalist who wanted capitalism and the wage system replaced by self-governing industries under a democratic state, with wide personal freedom of thought and sexual morals. He opposed conscription, Bolshevism and nationalism, wanted states to give up sovereignty over war to an international authority, and in old age led the campaign against nuclear weapons.

worker-ownership.rationale: Political Ideals (ch. 2) proposes replacing private capitalist enterprise with self-governing combinations of those who do the work; this is workers' control under state-fixed prices, not outright collective ownership.

workplace-democracy.rationale: He argues that workers have as much right to a voice in running their industry as citizens have in running the state, and that employers' concentration of initiative is a great evil (Political Ideals, ch. 2 and 4).

public-ownership.rationale: He calls state purchase of railways a typical state-socialist measure that would not cure the evils, preferring guild self-government, while wanting land held by the state; the record points both ways on state-owned industry.

state-harmful.rationale: He rejects anarchism and the abolition of the state: the state is needed to adjust relations between groups and to restrain private force (Political Ideals ch. 4; Roads to Freedom ch. 5).

property-fundamental.rationale: He holds that private property in land and capital lets owners use economic force and should be curtailed, with land probably under state ownership (Political Ideals, ch. 4).

property-serves-common-good.rationale: He says the state should satisfy itself that no owner holds more land than the public interest warrants and takes more than a just reward for labour (Political Ideals, ch. 4).

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: He condemns a system in which some are rich in idleness while others are poor despite unremitting labour, and wants the capitalist wage system replaced (Political Ideals, ch. 2).

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He argues that owners of land and capital use economic pressure as a form of force against the propertyless, and that the employer's power is a tyranny (Political Ideals ch. 4; Authority and the Individual).

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 2 says capitalism and the wage system 'must be abolished', to be replaced by self-governing industry; he still expects pay to continue within that system.

basic-income.rationale: Roads to Freedom (ch. 4) proposes a small income sufficient for necessaries secured to all whether they work or not, with more for those who do useful work.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: He says the only way to hold landholders to what the public interest warrants is probably state ownership of land, and wants the state to take all economic rent (Political Ideals, ch. 2 and 4).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He describes becoming a passionate Free Trader when Chamberlain advocated Protection in 1903 and stood on that line (Autobiography).

free-trade.rationale: In the Autobiography he calls himself a passionate Free Trader and records that free trade was the central issue of his 1907 Wimbledon campaign.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He wants the state to fix industry prices and abolish capitalism, yet also fears state-socialist monopoly of employment; his texts do not rank markets against government as such.

automate-paid-work.rationale: In Praise of Idleness argues that modern machinery could cut the working day to about four hours and that this should be the aim.

work-centre-of-life.rationale: In Praise of Idleness states that the morality of work is the morality of slaves and that the belief that work is virtuous causes great harm.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: He wants people to be free to work little for little pay and says unwillingness to work should be treated medically or educationally, not compelled (Political Ideals, ch. 2 and 4).

limit-population.rationale: Marriage and Morals treats population as a central problem and defends birth control so that families can be limited; he does not call for compulsory state limits.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Marriage and Morals (ch. on eugenics) backs sterilisation of the mentally defective as justified, but warns against broader laws such as Idaho's and against legislating before science is settled.

harm-principle.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 4 says the law should intervene only when injury is inflicted without the consent of the injured person, and leaves religion, opinion and private morals to individuals.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: He says organizations should take cognizance of no part of a man's life except possessions and the use of force, leaving the creative life to individual initiative (Political Ideals, ch. 4).

person-over-state.rationale: Political Ideals opens by saying politics must aim at the good of the individuals who compose the world, with nothing above or outside them to consider.

conscription.rationale: He says punishing conscientious objectors violates individual liberty and that the state cannot rightly compel men to use force against their belief (Political Ideals, ch. 4).

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Marriage and Morals attacks the obscenity law and its censorship of literature, including the banning of The Well of Loneliness, and Political Ideals condemns any censure of thought utterly.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Marriage and Morals argues that no law against obscenity can be framed without the harmful consequences he lists, and he opposes such censorship.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Political Ideals (ch. 1 and 4) wants diversity of character and says large organizations should leave the freest scope to originality; he does not speak of social pressure by name.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 4 says religion is not the state's business and that any censure of freedom of thought is to be condemned utterly.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 4 holds that a person's religion is of no public concern so long as the laws are obeyed; punishing a change of religion could not stand with this.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 4 says whether a man is Christian, Muslim or Jew is no public concern; legal limits on conversion contradict this.

assisted-dying.rationale: In 'Has Religion Made Useful Contributions to Civilization?' he describes a Lords bill to legalise euthanasia for painful incurable disease, with patient consent, as natural and mocks the Archbishop's objection.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: He judged the US ban on Mormon polygamy unwise and said the law should intervene only where injury is done without consent (Political Ideals, ch. 4).

premarital-sex.rationale: Marriage and Morals argues that equality of women implies no different sexual standard from men and criticises the demand that women alone be virgins before marriage.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Marriage and Morals condemns male domination for making marriage one of master and slave and calls for a marriage between equal partners.

women-suffrage.rationale: He stood in 1907 as a suffragist candidate at Wimbledon on a platform of the vote for women on the same terms as men (Autobiography).

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Marriage and Morals devotes discussion to sex education of children, arguing it should be given plainly and that ignorance and secrecy do harm.

traditional-family.rationale: He prizes stable marriage where there are children yet attacks the patriarchal family and traditional sexual morality, so his record on the traditional family points both ways (Marriage and Morals).

no-fault-divorce.rationale: He wants divorce on more grounds than English law allows and calls it right for childless couples, but doubts easy divorce where children are involved (Marriage and Morals).

more-religion-public.rationale: Education and the Social Order argues against institutional religion's hold on schools and against dogma taught as certain.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: He argues that religious instruction in schools harms young people by presenting doubtful propositions as certain; he does not set out the state-school rule in those words.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He says the realm of thought is unsuited to public control and the state should not force education into a uniform plan, which excludes official atheist teaching.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Human Society in Ethics and Politics argues scriptural precepts such as the witch commandment illustrate harmful taboo morality, and he rejects law grounded on them.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Human Society in Ethics and Politics cites 'Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live' as a harmful scriptural taboo, which he could not hold while treating scripture as inerrant.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Human Society in Ethics and Politics calls it feeble and contemptible to rely on comfortable myths one half knows to be myths, and he rests belief on evidence.

patriotic-education.rationale: Education and the Social Order has a chapter objecting to teaching patriotism in schools, saying it fosters nationalism that civilisation cannot survive.

character-from-environment.rationale: He says character results from the interaction of heredity and environment from conception on, and treats the proportion as undecided.

natural-rulers.rationale: In Unpopular Essays he attacks Plato's doctrine that the wise should rule as an aristocratic prejudice dressed in philosophy and calls the Republic a totalitarian tract.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Authority and the Individual says large democracies give scope for political initiative to a tiny minority and proposes giving workers and local bodies real control.

decide-locally.rationale: Authority and the Individual states that smaller bodies should keep all functions that do not prevent larger bodies from fulfilling their purpose, a principle he also applies in Political Ideals.

democracy-best.rationale: In the Bolshevism book he defends democratic government as the method that spares civil war and defends self-government on three stated grounds, while not idealising Parliament.

one-party-rule.rationale: In Practice and Theory of Bolshevism he describes Communist Party monopoly of power, crushed opposition and suppressed free speech, and judges it unlikely to yield a desirable order.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: He rejects the method of violent revolution and Communist dictatorship as unlikely to produce a stable or desirable society (Bolshevism book, ch. 4 and 7).

party-controls-media.rationale: He reports the whole Russian press as official and free speech completely suppressed, and treats this as a serious evil of Bolshevism.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He records that opposition in Soviet Russia was crushed without mercy and ranks this among the evils making Bolshevism unlikely to succeed.

separate-church-state.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 4 holds religion is a matter in which the state should not interfere, though he allows exceptions such as banning human sacrifice.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 5 calls for an international government that is legislative as well as judicial, with the only army and navy in the world.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He argues states must part with absolute sovereignty in external relations in favour of an international instrument of government; the EU is not named.

nation-first.rationale: He says a man's actions in matters of concern to other nations should take account of the universal welfare, not group interest (Political Ideals, ch. 5).

national-self-determination.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 5 says each nation should be self-governing in internal affairs and that national boundaries should coincide with state boundaries with very few exceptions.

national-law-over-international.rationale: He calls a state's claim to absolute sovereignty in external affairs primitive anarchy and says international authority must decide such questions (Political Ideals, ch. 5).

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Political Ideals ch. 5 expects a growing practice of submitting disputes to arbitration and wants an international authority to decide between states.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He says the international authority's army and navy should be the only ones in existence, so that states hold none (Political Ideals, ch. 5).

arms-reduction.rationale: Common Sense and Nuclear Warfare argues for agreed reduction of nuclear and other armaments by East and West as the way to survival.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: He advocated practically that Britain renounce its H-bombs, saying this would not measurably change the balance (Common Sense and Nuclear Warfare, appendix I).

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: In the appendix to Common Sense and Nuclear Warfare he says British renunciation of H-bombs would have no measurable effect on the balance, and he urges it.

defeat-communism.rationale: From the mid-1950s he urged coexistence and agreements between East and West and called the view that no world is better than a Communist one insane; after 1945 he had briefly urged firmness (SEP).

civil-disobedience-accept-penalty.rationale: He took part in mass civil disobedience in the Committee of 100 and served jail terms in 1918 and 1961, but his texts here do not state a rule that penalties must be accepted.

notes: Searched his own books on economy, liberty, sex and family, religion in schools, world government, war and nuclear weapons, Soviet Russia, women's suffrage and free trade; the record is mostly 1914-1960 and many modern statements (technology, climate, identity, immigration) have no position. After 1945 he briefly urged firm pressure on the USSR (SEP) but from the mid-1950s urged coexistence and unilateral British nuclear renunciation, which is the later, sustained position used. He called himself not a complete pacifist and backed the WWII effort; no statement on that war's justification is recorded as an answer.
